Democratic candidates for Office in Arlington yesterday charged their G.O.P. opponents with resorting to smear tactics, building straw men and refusing to deal with the facts in the current election campaign. J. Maynard Magruder, running for county treasurer, took aim on Republican incumbent Colin C. MacPherson, who Monday night linked the Democratic candidate with a service charge received by former treasurer John Locke Green on a loan from a bank in which county funds were deposited.

The question was a campaign issue in 1851 when Mr. MacPherson defeated Mr. Green, running as an independent, for the treasurer's post.

At a luncheon meeting of the Arlington Women's Democratic Club, Mr. Magruder said a jury had assessed $500 damages against Mr. MacPherson in a civil damage suit growing out of the allegations against Mr. Green. The State Supreme Court of Appeals later reversed this award.

Mr. Magruder said the 1851 incident involved two Republicans, Mr. MacPherson and Mr. Green, and that he had never been a Republican himself. Mr. Green, once a Republican, stated he left the party seven or eight years ago.

"I share neither Mr. Green's ideas nor his ideals," Mr. Magruder added, "what was done was pure and simple business transaction."

Commemorative Attorney William J. Hassan also scored what he termed a "Republican campaign of smear, vilification and character assassination."

The Democratic incumbent said that a woman, whom he declined to identify, had received a call from another Arlington woman charging that "scandalous activities involving young women are going on in the Commonwealth Attorney's office at night."

Mr. Hassan categorically denied the allegations as he has reports of improper handling of leases made by G.O.P. candidate W. Wynne Tolbert.

Other Democratic candidates speaking at the luncheon included incumbent State Senator Charles R. Fenwick, revenue commissioner George D. Fischer, unopposed; incumbent Sheriff Carl Taylor, unopposed; County Judge Paul Brown, and House of Delegates candidate William H. Winston.

WASHINGTON, R— "The important thing to remember," says Harry S. Truman, "is that the President is the only person in the executive branch who has final authority, and if he does not exercise it we may be in trouble!"

And so out of his cabinet in the aftermath of World War II went Secretary of State James F. Byrnes, Secretary of Commerce Henry A. Wallace and Secretary of the Interior Harold L. Ickes. They all, in Truman's opinion and his own phrase, got too big for their breeches.

The former President tells the story in the current installment of his memoirs, published in Life magazine. Most of this has been told before but there are some new sidelights—notably a feeling by Truman in 1946 that Wallace might well become a tool of the Communists.

Truman fired Wallace for making a speech critical of administration foreign policy. He tells of calling the then Secretary of Commerce to his office and listening to Wallace lecture on "the beauty of peace."

"I have never doubted Henry Wallace's sincerity or honesty of purpose," Truman says, "but after this conversation I was afraid that knowingly or not, he would lend himself to the more sinister ends."

ATLANTIC CITY, N. J., Feb. 1.—The churches may prove to be the main bastion for freedom in our country, a leading Lutheran minister declared today.

DR. Oscar A. Benson of Minneapolis, president of the National Lutheran Council, asserted that "in a time when freedom of speech and even freedom of thought are jeopardized by those who have the power to intimidate and to apply social and economic pressures, it may be that the church remains as the staunchest defender of our American liberties."

DR. Benson, also president of the Augustana Lutheran Church, made the statement in his report at the opening session of the council's 37th annual meeting.

8 Churches Represented.

Delegates representing eight Lutheran church bodies, totaling 8 million members, are attending the meeting at Cotton Manor Hotel. Denominations in the council, organized in 1918, are the United Lutheran Church in America, 2,142,000 members; Evangelical Lutheran Church, $4,000; American Lutheran Church, 1,926,900; Augustana Lutheran Church, 1,000,000; Lutheran Free Church, $4,000; United Evangelical Lutheran Church, $4,000; Finnish Evangelical Lutheran Church, $1,000, and American Evangelical Lutheran Church, $1,000.

DR. Benson asserted that "the perpetuation of our freedoms will ultimately depend not so much on patriotic oratory in and out of Congress as on the attitudes we develop in the hearts of our youth, whether those young people are in uniform or in classrooms."

Elections Today.

DR. Benson probably will be reelected to his third consecutive one-year term as council president today. DR. Henry F. Schuh of Columbus, Ohio, president of the American Lutheran Church, probably will be chosen for his third consecutive term as vice president.

Both DR. F. Eppling Reinartz of New York, secretary of the United Lutheran Church, and Fred C. Eggerstedt of Richmond Hill, Long Island, N. Y., are expected to be returned as secretary and treasurer, respectively.
